2005-Q15a.q: Comment on why viruses are hard to classify as living. (2 points)
2005-Q15a.right: Not made of cells; can only reproduce inside a host cell
wrong: Not made of cells; reproduce by binary fission
Contain both DNA and RNA; reproduce inside hosts
Have organelles but no nucleus; reproduce alone
2005-Q15a.why: Two points: viruses are non-cellular and can reproduce only in a host cell; they also have just one nucleic acid and no organelles.
2005-Q15a.hint: Think about what all living things are built from, and whether a virus can copy itself alone.

2005-Q15a.q: Name two diseases of humans caused by viruses. (2 points)
wrong: Measles and tuberculosis
Tetanus and the common cold
Athlete's foot and cholera
2005-Q15a.why: Two points: any two viral diseases, e.g. measles, colds, flu, polio, mumps, AIDS; TB, tetanus and cholera are bacterial, athlete's foot fungal.
2005-Q15a.hint: Think of illnesses antibiotics can't treat, like winter sniffles, or ones childhood jabs prevent.

2005-Q15a.q: Name two lymphocytes and give a role of each against microbes. (4 points)
2005-Q15a.right: B cells make antibodies; killer T cells destroy infected cells
wrong: B cells burst infected cells; T cells make antibodies
B cells engulf microbes; killer T cells make antibodies
Monocytes engulf microbes; red cells carry antibodies
2005-Q15a.why: Four points: two lymphocytes named, each with a matching role: B cells make antibodies; killer T cells destroy infected cells.
2005-Q15a.hint: There are two letter-named kinds: which one makes the Y-shaped proteins, and what does the other do?

2005-Q15a.q: Is vaccine immunity like immunity after an infection, and why?
2005-Q15a.right: Yes: both make the body produce antibodies
wrong: No: a vaccine gives ready-made antibodies
No: only an infection makes memory cells
Yes: both of them give passive immunity
2005-Q15a.why: Both expose you to the antigen, so your own lymphocytes make antibodies and memory cells: active immunity.
2005-Q15a.hint: In both cases the body meets the antigen. What do your own lymphocytes then make?

2005-Q15b.q: What does it mean to call a bacterium pathogenic?
2005-Q15b.right: It causes disease in its host
wrong: It feeds on dead organic matter
It makes its own food
It is resistant to antibiotics
2005-Q15b.why: Pathogenic means disease-causing; a bacterium that feeds on dead matter is a saprophyte.
2005-Q15b.hint: 'Patho-' means suffering and '-genic' means producing. What does such a bacterium do to its host?

2005-Q15b.q: What are antibiotics, and why is misusing them dangerous? (3 points)
2005-Q15b.right: Made by microbes to kill bacteria; resistant strains survive
wrong: Made by B cells to kill bacteria; you become immune to them
Made by microbes to kill viruses; bacteria learn to resist
Made by microbes to kill bacteria; resistant ones die first
2005-Q15b.why: Three points: antibiotics are made by micro-organisms and stop bacteria or fungi growing; misuse lets resistant strains survive and build up.
2005-Q15b.hint: Where did penicillin come from, and what does it attack? Then, which bacteria survive a dose?

2006-Q6e.q: Explain the terms antigen and antibody. (2 points)
2006-Q6e.right: Antigen: on a microbe's surface; antibody: made against it
wrong: Antibody: on a microbe's surface; antigen: made against it
Antigen: a drug from fungi; antibody: a protein on bacteria
Antigen: a white blood cell; antibody: made by the microbe
2006-Q6e.why: Two points: an antigen is a substance on the surface of a cell, virus or bacterium; an antibody is a protein made in response to it.
2006-Q6e.hint: Antigen is short for 'antibody generator'. Which one sits on the invader, and which is the reply?

2006-Q15b.q: What are antibiotics and what are they used for? (2 points)
2006-Q15b.right: Made by microbes; used to treat infections
wrong: Made by lymphocytes; used to fight infections
Weakened microbes; used to give immunity
Made by the body; used to kill viruses
2006-Q15b.why: Two points: antibiotics are made by bacteria or fungi, and used to treat infections; antibodies are what your own body makes.
2006-Q15b.hint: Penicillin came from a mould. Where do these drugs come from, and when does a doctor prescribe them?

2006-Q15b.q: What is antibiotic resistance and how may it develop? (2 points)
2006-Q15b.right: Bacteria survive the antibiotic; arises by natural selection
wrong: Patient becomes immune to the drug; arises by vaccination
Bacteria survive it; arises as bacteria learn to resist
Antibodies stop working; arises by natural selection
2006-Q15b.why: Two points: resistant bacteria aren't killed or inhibited by the antibiotic; it develops by natural selection as resistant ones survive.
2006-Q15b.hint: If a drug kills most bacteria but a few live on and breed, which of Darwin's ideas is at work?

2006-Q15c.q: Write about the biological benefits of breastfeeding. (3 points)
2006-Q15c.right: Passes antibodies, right nutrients, right temperature
wrong: Passes antibodies, active immunity, earlier ovulation
Right nutrients, right temperature, contains antibiotics
Passes antibodies, stops the uterus contracting, warm milk
2006-Q15c.why: Three points: milk passes on antibodies (passive immunity), has the right nutrients and is at the right temperature; it also delays ovulation.
2006-Q15c.hint: Think of protection passed on from mum, the food value of the milk, and how it's served.

2007-Q14b.q: Comment on the difficulty of defining viruses as living. (2 points)
2007-Q14b.right: Only reproduce inside a host cell; not made of cells
wrong: Reproduce alone by binary fission; not made of cells
Only reproduce in hosts; have their own ribosomes
Make their own energy; have both DNA and RNA
2007-Q14b.why: Two points: viruses are obligate parasites (only reproduce in a host cell) and non-cellular; they also have no metabolism of their own.
2007-Q14b.hint: Compare a virus with the signs of life: can it reproduce alone, and what is it built from?

2007-Q14b.q: What two substances make up a virus particle?
wrong: Lipid and carbohydrate
Cellulose and chitin
Starch and phospholipid
2007-Q14b.why: A virus is just a protein coat around a core of nucleic acid, either DNA or RNA.
2007-Q14b.hint: Think of a virus as genes wrapped in a coat. What is each of those two parts made of?

2007-Q14b.q: Name two diseases caused by viruses. (2 points)
wrong: Polio and cholera
Ringworm and measles
Tetanus and TB
2007-Q14b.why: Two points: any two viral diseases, e.g. polio, measles, flu, colds; cholera, tetanus and TB are bacterial, and ringworm is fungal.
2007-Q14b.hint: Think of illnesses antibiotics can't help with, or ones babies get routine jabs against.

2007-Q14b.q: Which is a beneficial use of viruses?
wrong: Making antibiotics like penicillin
Making yoghurt and cheese
Fixing nitrogen in the soil
2007-Q14b.why: Viruses can carry genes into cells, so they're used as vectors; penicillin comes from a fungus, not a virus.
2007-Q14b.hint: Viruses naturally inject genetic material into cells. How could scientists make use of that?

2007-Q14b.right: A microbe-made chemical that kills bacteria
wrong: A protein made by B cells against antigens
A harmless dose of a pathogen
A chemical the body makes to kill viruses
2007-Q14b.why: Two points: antibiotics are made by micro-organisms (bacteria or fungi) and kill or stop the growth of other micro-organisms.
2007-Q14b.hint: Think of penicillin: what kind of living thing first made it, and what does it do to germs?

2007-Q14b.q: Why not give antibiotics for a viral infection?
2007-Q14b.right: Antibiotics have no effect on viruses
wrong: Antibiotics kill viruses too slowly
Antibiotics make the virus multiply
Viruses are killed by vaccines instead
2007-Q14b.why: Antibiotics act on bacteria (and fungi), not viruses; giving them anyway just helps resistant bacteria build up.
2007-Q14b.hint: Antibiotics target parts that bacteria have. Does a virus have any of those parts?

2007-Q14c.q: What does the word immunity mean?
wrong: Being more likely to catch an infection
Taking antibiotics to clear an infection
Having no microbes living on the body
2007-Q14c.why: Immunity is the ability to resist infection, usually because antibodies and memory cells are ready for the antigen.
2007-Q14c.hint: If you're immune to chickenpox, what happens when you meet it again?

2007-Q14c.q: What is the main job of B lymphocytes?
wrong: Burst infected cells using perforin
Engulf bacteria by phagocytosis
Switch off the immune response
2007-Q14c.why: B cells recognise a specific antigen and make antibodies (and memory cells); bursting infected cells is a killer T job.
2007-Q14c.hint: What Y-shaped proteins do B cells release when they meet an antigen that matches them?

2007-Q14c.q: Distinguish between active and passive immunity. (2 points)
2007-Q14c.right: Active: body makes antibodies; passive: antibodies put in
wrong: Active: antibodies put in; passive: body makes them
Active: body makes antibiotics; passive: antibodies put in
Active: from vaccines only; passive: from infections only
2007-Q14c.why: Two points: in active immunity the body makes its own antibodies; in passive immunity ready-made antibodies are put into the body.
2007-Q14c.hint: Compare a vaccinated person with a breastfed baby: where do the antibodies come from in each?

2007-Q14c.q: Why does a vaccine give active immunity?
2007-Q14c.right: Its antigens make the body produce antibodies
wrong: It injects ready-made antibodies into you
It contains antibiotics that kill the germ
It adds donor white blood cells to the blood
2007-Q14c.why: A vaccine brings in a harmless antigen, and your own lymphocytes respond by making antibodies: that's active.
2007-Q14c.hint: What does a vaccine carry into the body, and how do your own lymphocytes respond to it?

2007-Q14c.q: Being given a specific antibody is which type of immunity?
wrong: Active
Innate
Inherited
2007-Q14c.why: The antibodies are made outside your body and given ready-made, so it's passive; active means your body makes them.
2007-Q14c.hint: Did your own body make that antibody, or did it arrive ready-made?

2007-Q14c.q: When might an antibody be given instead of a vaccine?
2007-Q14c.right: When infection may already have happened
wrong: When lifelong protection is needed
When the person is already immune
When the patient is allergic to antibiotics
2007-Q14c.why: Antibodies work at once, which helps if someone may already be infected and there's no time for a vaccine to work.
2007-Q14c.hint: A vaccine takes a week or more to work. When would there be no time to wait?

2007-Q14c.q: How long does immunity from a given antibody last?
2007-Q14c.right: Short: weeks to a few months
wrong: Lifelong, like after an infection
Many years, like a vaccine
Longer than active immunity
2007-Q14c.why: The given antibodies are broken down and no memory cells are made, so the protection soon fades.
2007-Q14c.hint: Donated antibodies are broken down and no memory cells are made. So how long can it last?

2008-Q6d.q: Which is a biological advantage of breastfeeding?
2008-Q6d.right: Milk is sterile and at the right temperature
wrong: Milk contains antibiotics for the baby
It gives the baby active immunity
It makes ovulation return sooner
2008-Q6d.why: Breast milk is sterile, at body temperature and full of antibodies; those give passive, not active, immunity.
2008-Q6d.hint: Think about protection from germs, nutrition, and why milk straight from mum needs no preparing.

2008-Q15b.q: Why did myxomatosis kill so many rabbits at first? (2 points)
2008-Q15b.right: No immunity in the population, and fleas spread it rapidly
wrong: Rabbits had memory cells for it, and fleas spread it fast
No immunity, and the virus could reproduce outside cells
No immunity, and antibiotics made the virus stronger
2008-Q15b.why: Two points: the virus was new, so the population had no immunity, and suitable vectors (fleas) spread it rapidly.
2008-Q15b.hint: The virus was brand new to Ireland. What did the rabbits lack, and how did it travel between them?

2008-Q15b.q: Why is myxomatosis less of a threat to Irish rabbits now?
2008-Q15b.right: Natural selection: resistant rabbits survived and bred
wrong: All wild rabbits are now vaccinated against it
Antibiotics now cure the disease in rabbits
The virus has died out completely in Ireland
2008-Q15b.why: Rabbits with natural immunity survived and passed it on (natural selection); antibiotics don't work on viruses.
2008-Q15b.hint: A few rabbits survived the first outbreak. What did they pass on to their young?

2008-Q15b.q: Which is a sound reason for your answer on the HIV trend?
2008-Q15b.right: Yes: resistant people survive and have children
wrong: No: antibiotics will soon wipe out HIV
No: the HIV virus is unable to mutate
Yes: antibiotics will make people immune
2008-Q15b.why: Natural selection works on humans too, just slowly; HIV is a virus that mutates, and antibiotics don't touch it.
2008-Q15b.hint: Could this happen in humans? Recall how the rabbits recovered, then think about the timescale.

2008-Q15b.q: Outline briefly how a virus replicates. (3 points)
2008-Q15b.right: Attaches, injects DNA or RNA, which the host cell copies
wrong: Attaches, injects its protein coat, which divides in two
Attaches, injects DNA, which its own ribosomes copy
Splits by binary fission, then injects DNA into a new host
2008-Q15b.why: Three points: the virus attaches to a host cell, introduces its DNA or RNA, and uses the host's resources to copy it and assemble new viruses.
2008-Q15b.hint: Step by step: how does it latch on, what goes inside, and whose machinery does the copying?

2009-Q15c.q: Write about the role of lymphocytes. (3 points)
2009-Q15c.right: B cells make antibodies; T cells kill infected cells
wrong: B cells burst infected cells; T cells make antibodies
B cells make antibodies; T cells engulf bacteria
B cells make antibiotics; T cells carry oxygen
2009-Q15c.why: Three points: lymphocytes are part of the immune system; B cells make antibodies; T cells do jobs like killing infected cells.
2009-Q15c.hint: Which kind of lymphocyte releases Y-shaped proteins, and what jobs do the other kinds do?

2009-Q15c.q: Write about the economic and medical importance of viruses. (3 points)
2009-Q15c.right: Damage crops; cause flu; used in genetic engineering
wrong: Damage crops; make penicillin; fix nitrogen for farmers
Used to brew beer; cause flu; used in genetic engineering
Damage crops; cause cholera; used to make yoghurt
2009-Q15c.why: Three points, at least one of each: economic, e.g. crop or livestock damage; medical, e.g. diseases like flu, or use in genetic engineering.
2009-Q15c.hint: Think of costs to farming, illnesses they cause in people, and how scientists can put them to work.

2010-Q6.q: What is part A on the diagram made of?
wrong: Lipid
Carbohydrate
Nucleic acid
2010-Q6.why: The coat and other outer parts of a virus are protein; the nucleic acid (part B) is the genetic material inside.
2010-Q6.hint: A is the virus's outer coat. Which biomolecule, the same type as enzymes, builds it?

2010-Q6.q: What is part B on the diagram made of?
wrong: Protein
Lipid
Carbohydrate
2010-Q6.why: B is the virus's genetic material: a nucleic acid, either DNA or RNA, wrapped in the protein coat.
2010-Q6.hint: B is the genetic material at the core. What type of biomolecule carries genes?

2010-Q6.q: Briefly describe how viruses reproduce. (3 points)
2010-Q6.right: Attaches, injects nucleic acid, uses host structures
wrong: Attaches, injects nucleic acid, then splits in two
Attaches, injects its protein coat, uses host structures
Enters the cell, uses its own ribosomes to make parts
2010-Q6.why: Three points: the virus attaches, injects its nucleic acid, and uses the host's structures to copy its parts, which assemble and are released.
2010-Q6.hint: Start with the virus landing on the cell, then what it sends inside, then who builds the copies.

2010-Q6.q: Why were younger people more at risk from swine flu? (2 points)
2010-Q6.right: Older people had earlier exposure, so already had antibodies
wrong: Younger people had earlier exposure, so had more antibodies
Older people took antibiotics, which killed the virus
Young people can't make antibodies until adulthood
2010-Q6.why: Two points: older people had probably been exposed to a similar flu before, so they already had antibodies and memory cells for it.
2010-Q6.hint: Older people have lived through more flu seasons. What might their immune systems already have?

2010-Q15c.q: Why won't doctors give antibiotics for a cold?
2010-Q15c.right: A cold is viral; antibiotics don't affect viruses
wrong: A cold is caused by a fungus, not bacteria
Antibiotics make the cold virus resistant
Antibiotics stop you making antibodies
2010-Q15c.why: Colds are caused by viruses, which antibiotics can't touch; overusing them also breeds resistant bacteria.
2010-Q15c.hint: What kind of microbe causes a cold, and what kind do antibiotics act on?

2011-Q10b.q: Why might deaths from a virus fall over the years?
wrong: Antibiotics start to work on it
Hosts lose their antibodies to it
The virus stops being a parasite
2011-Q10b.why: Over time the population builds immunity (natural selection favours resistant hosts), so fewer die.
2011-Q10b.hint: Think about the survivors of each outbreak, and what they and their offspring may now have.

2012-Q15b.q: State two ways, other than colour, red blood cells differ from white. (2 points)
2012-Q15b.right: No nucleus when mature, and contain haemoglobin
wrong: No nucleus, and larger than white cells
Have a nucleus, and fewer of them in blood
Contain haemoglobin, and make antibodies
2012-Q15b.why: Two points: red cells have no nucleus and contain haemoglobin to carry oxygen; they're also smaller, biconcave and far more numerous.
2012-Q15b.hint: Compare what's inside each cell, their size and shape, and how many there are in blood.

2012-Q15b.q: Which group of white blood cells is NOT a type of lymphocyte?
wrong: B cells
Killer T cells
Platelets
2012-Q15b.why: Monocytes are phagocytes that engulf microbes; B and T cells are lymphocytes, and platelets aren't white cells.
2012-Q15b.hint: Think of the white cells that engulf and eat germs rather than making antibodies.

2012-Q15b.q: What do antibodies do in the body?
2012-Q15b.right: Bind to antigens and inactivate them
wrong: Engulf microbes by phagocytosis
Burst infected cells with perforin
Release antibiotics to kill bacteria
2012-Q15b.why: Antibodies lock onto a specific antigen and inactivate it, for example by clumping or bursting the microbe.
2012-Q15b.hint: Antibodies match one antigen like a key in a lock. What do they do to it once attached?

2012-Q15b.q: Which list has three types of T cell?
wrong: Helper, killer, plasma
Killer, memory, B cell
Helper, suppressor, phagocyte
2012-Q15b.why: The four T cell types are helper, killer, suppressor and memory; B cells and phagocytes are different white cells.
2012-Q15b.hint: T cells are named after their jobs: think of support, attack, switching off and recall.

2012-Q15b.q: Give a role for helper, killer and suppressor T cells, in that order. (3 points)
2012-Q15b.right: Recognise antigens; kill infected cells; stop the response
wrong: Make antibodies; kill infected cells; stop the response
Recognise antigens; stop the response; kill infected cells
Engulf bacteria; make antibodies; remember the antigen
2012-Q15b.why: Three points: helper T cells recognise antigens, killer T cells attack infected cells, suppressor T cells stop the immune response.
2012-Q15b.hint: Each T cell's name tells you its job. Think about the start, the middle and the end of an attack.

2013-Q12a.q: What evidence fits a virus being 'escaped genetic material'?
2013-Q12a.right: It is made of nucleic acid (DNA or RNA)
wrong: It has its own nucleus and membrane
It can respire and grow on its own
It is made of cellulose and lipid
2013-Q12a.why: A virus is basically DNA or RNA in a protein coat, like a stray bit of a cell's genes.
2013-Q12a.hint: Look under the virus's coat. What's in there, and where else would you find that in a cell?

2013-Q12a.q: Why are viruses called obligate parasites?
2013-Q12a.right: They can only reproduce inside a host cell
wrong: They always kill their host straight away
They feed on dead and decaying matter
They can reproduce in or out of a cell
2013-Q12a.why: 'Obligate' means they have no choice: viruses can only reproduce using a living host cell's machinery.
2013-Q12a.hint: 'Obligate' means it has no choice. Where must a virus be in order to make copies of itself?

2013-Q12a.q: How can a virus be useful to people?
wrong: Used to make penicillin
Used to make yoghurt
Used to make bread rise
2013-Q12a.why: Viruses are used in cancer treatment and genetic engineering; penicillin, yoghurt and bread need fungi or bacteria.
2013-Q12a.hint: Viruses are experts at getting genes into cells. How could scientists or doctors use that?

2013-Q12c.q: Which statement about antibodies and antibiotics is right? (one of 4 points)
2013-Q12c.right: Antibodies are proteins made by the body
wrong: Antibodies are made by fungi to kill bacteria
Antibiotics are made by B lymphocytes
Antibiotics kill viruses as well as bacteria
2013-Q12c.why: Four points: antibodies are proteins made by the body against antigens; antibiotics are made by microbes, kill other microbes, not viruses.
2013-Q12c.hint: For each one ask: who makes it, what is it made of or what does it do, and does it work on viruses?

2013-Q12c.q: Distinguish active and passive immunity in terms of antibodies. (2 points)
2013-Q12c.right: Active: body makes antibodies; passive: antibodies given
wrong: Active: antibodies given; passive: body makes its own
Active: antibiotics given; passive: body makes antibodies
Both: the body makes its own antibodies after a vaccine
2013-Q12c.why: Two points: in active immunity your body makes its own antibodies; in passive immunity ready-made antibodies are given (e.g. in breast milk).
2013-Q12c.hint: For each type, ask: did your own cells make the antibodies, or were they handed over ready-made?

2013-Q12c.q: Why is an infection more likely in hospital than at home? (2 points)
2013-Q12c.right: Antibiotic-resistant strains are common; patients are weaker
wrong: Resistant strains are common; patients are stronger
Antibiotics there destroy patients' antibodies
Vaccines given there spread the disease to patients
2013-Q12c.why: Two points: heavy antibiotic use selects resistant strains (like MRSA), and patients are weaker; there are also more pathogens and people.
2013-Q12c.hint: Think about how much antibiotic is used in a hospital, and how healthy the people there are.

2014-Q15b.q: Why did Australia's rabbit numbers recover?
2014-Q15b.right: Rabbits evolved immunity to the virus
wrong: Antibiotics cured the infected rabbits
Farmers vaccinated the wild rabbits
The virus could not infect European rabbits
2014-Q15b.why: The few rabbits with resistance survived and bred, so natural selection built up an immune population.
2014-Q15b.hint: Some rabbits survived the virus. What did they have that the others lacked, and pass on?

2015-Q3.q: What is part A of the virus mainly made of?
wrong: Carbohydrate
Nucleic acid
Cellulose
2015-Q3.why: Part A is made mainly of protein, like every virus coat; the nucleic acid (B) is the genetic material.
2015-Q3.hint: A is the coat around the virus. It's the same kind of biomolecule as enzymes and keratin.

2015-Q3.q: What does 'obligate parasite' mean for a virus?
2015-Q3.right: It can only replicate using a living cell
wrong: It can replicate inside or outside a cell
It must always kill the cell it enters
It lives on dead matter outside cells
2015-Q3.why: A virus has no machinery of its own, so it can only make copies of itself inside a host cell.
2015-Q3.hint: 'Obligate' means 'no choice'. What can't a virus do without getting inside something living?

2015-Q3.q: Part B is one of two possible molecules. Which one?
wrong: Protein
Lipid
Carbohydrate
2015-Q3.why: Part B is the genetic material: either DNA or RNA, never both, inside the protein coat.
2015-Q3.hint: B is the virus's genetic material. Which two molecules can carry genes? Name either one.

2015-Q3.q: Which virus causes disease in plants?
wrong: Influenza virus
Myxoma virus
Measles virus
2015-Q3.why: Tobacco mosaic virus blotches the leaves of plants; flu, measles and myxoma viruses infect animals.
2015-Q3.hint: Think of the virus named after the patchy, tiled pattern it makes on a plant's leaves.

2015-Q3.q: How do scientists tell different viruses apart?
2015-Q3.right: By the shape of their protein coat
wrong: By the type of nucleus they have
By how they carry out respiration
By staining their cell walls
2015-Q3.why: Viruses differ in coat shape, size and type of nucleic acid; they have no nucleus, cell wall or respiration.
2015-Q3.hint: Under an electron microscope, what's the first thing you'd notice about a virus's outside?

2015-Q3.q: Why don't viruses fit into any kingdom?
2015-Q3.right: They are not made of cells
wrong: They contain both DNA and RNA
They are all prokaryotic cells
They make their own food
2015-Q3.why: Kingdoms group cellular organisms; viruses have no cells or organelles, so they don't fit.
2015-Q3.hint: Every kingdom is made of living things built from the same basic unit. Does a virus have it?

2015-Q3.q: Which is one economic importance of viruses?
wrong: Used to brew beer and wine
Used to produce penicillin
Used to make biogas from waste
2015-Q3.why: Viruses are used to make vaccines and can harm crops and livestock; penicillin, beer and biogas use fungi or bacteria.
2015-Q3.hint: Think of what drug companies grow viruses to make, or of harm done to crops and farm animals.

2015-Q14a.q: Which pairs a general defence with how it works? (2 points)
2015-Q14a.right: Mucus traps microbes; cilia sweep it away
wrong: Skin makes antibodies to stop microbes
Phagocytes burst cells with perforin
Clotting releases antibodies into wounds
2015-Q14a.why: Two points: the feature and how it works: mucus in the airways traps microbes and cilia sweep them out. Antibodies are specific.
2015-Q14a.hint: Pick a barrier germs meet first, like skin or the airway lining. How does it keep them out?

2015-Q14a.q: Name two organs specific to the immune system. (2 points)
wrong: Thymus and thyroid
Kidney and spleen
Thyroid and pancreas
2015-Q14a.why: Two points: any two of thymus, spleen, lymph nodes and tonsils; the thyroid, pancreas and kidneys are not immune organs.
2015-Q14a.hint: Think of where lymphocytes mature or gather: a gland in the chest, an organ beside the stomach.

2015-Q14a.right: A protein made in response to an antigen
wrong: A foreign molecule that triggers immunity
A chemical made by fungi to kill bacteria
A white blood cell that engulfs germs
2015-Q14a.why: Antibodies are proteins made by B cells against a specific antigen; the antigen is the foreign molecule itself.
2015-Q14a.hint: One is the foreign marker that sets off a response; the other is your body's reply. Which is which?

2015-Q14a.q: Describe the roles of killer T cells and helper T cells. (2 points)
2015-Q14a.right: Killer: recognise infected cells; helper: produce interferon
wrong: Killer: make antibodies; helper: switch off the response
Killer: recognise infected cells; helper: make antibodies
Killer: switch off the response; helper: engulf bacteria
2015-Q14a.why: Two points: killer T cells recognise infected (or cancer) cells and burst them; helper T cells produce interferon and stimulate B cells.
2015-Q14a.hint: Which of your own cells do killer T cells hunt? And which other cells do helpers switch on?

2015-Q14a.q: Which T cells stop the immune response?
wrong: Helper T cells
Killer T cells
Memory T cells
2015-Q14a.why: Suppressor (regulatory) T cells switch the immune response off once the infection has been cleared.
2015-Q14a.hint: Which T cell's name means to hold something down or keep it under control?

wrong: A chemical that kills bacteria
A protein that fights an infection
A microbe that breaks down dead matter
2015-Q15c.why: A pathogen is anything that causes disease, like a disease-causing bacterium, virus, fungus or prion.
2015-Q15c.hint: Break the word up: '-gen' means 'to produce', as in generate. What does a pathogen produce?

2016-Q15c.q: Which pairs a viral disease with a sign of it?
2016-Q15c.right: Measles: red rash and high fever
wrong: Tuberculosis: long-lasting cough
Common cold: rash all over the body
Polio: yellowing of skin and eyes
2016-Q15c.why: Measles is viral and shows as a red rash with fever; TB is bacterial, and yellow skin is a sign of hepatitis.
2016-Q15c.hint: Pick an illness caused by a virus, then think of the signs a doctor would spot first.

2016-Q15c.q: What is the biological basis of vaccination?
2016-Q15c.right: It stimulates the body to make antibodies
wrong: It gives the body ready-made antibodies
It kills pathogens already in the blood
It contains antibiotics that kill germs
2016-Q15c.why: A vaccine's antigen stimulates your lymphocytes to make antibodies and memory cells: active immunity.
2016-Q15c.hint: A vaccine carries a harmless antigen. How do your lymphocytes react when they meet it?

2017-Q4.q: What is meant by a pathogen?
wrong: An organism that feeds on dead matter
An organism that makes its own food
An organism that needs no oxygen
2017-Q4.why: Pathogen means disease-causing; an organism that feeds on dead matter is a saprophyte, not a pathogen.
2017-Q4.hint: The Greek 'pathos' means suffering. What does a pathogen do to whatever it infects?

2017-Q4.right: Microbe-made chemical that kills other microbes
wrong: Body-made protein that targets antigens
Weakened microbe that gives immunity
Chemical that kills microbes on surfaces
2017-Q4.why: Antibiotics like penicillin are made by microbes (fungi or bacteria) and kill or stop the growth of other microbes.
2017-Q4.hint: Penicillin was found growing from a mould. What makes antibiotics, and what do they do to bacteria?

2017-Q14a.q: Why were pregnant women told to avoid Zika areas?
2017-Q14a.right: Zika may cause microcephaly in babies
wrong: Pregnant women cannot make antibodies
Zika is quickly fatal to pregnant women
Antibiotics for Zika harm unborn babies
2017-Q14a.why: The passage links Zika to microcephaly, where babies have small heads, so pregnant women were warned off.
2017-Q14a.hint: Reread the passage: what condition in newborn babies is being linked to Zika?

2017-Q14a.q: Give two precautions against Zika if travelling to affected areas. (2 points)
2017-Q14a.right: Use mosquito nets and repellent; use condoms during sex
wrong: Take antibiotics before you go; drink only bottled water
Use mosquito nets; take antibiotics to kill the virus
Go out mostly at dawn and dusk; try for a baby soon
2017-Q14a.why: Two points: avoid mosquito bites (nets, repellent, long sleeves) and use condoms or delay pregnancy, as Zika also spreads by sex.
2017-Q14a.hint: The passage says what carries Zika and when it bites. How do you avoid bites, and protect a baby?

2017-Q14a.q: Which is an example of a beneficial virus?
wrong: Penicillium, which makes penicillin
Rhizobium, which fixes nitrogen
Yeast, which makes bread rise
2017-Q14a.why: Bacteriophages are viruses that infect and kill bacteria; Penicillium and yeast are fungi and Rhizobium is a bacterium.
2017-Q14a.hint: Some viruses attack bacteria rather than us. How could that help, and what are they called?

2017-Q14a.q: After new virus parts are made in the host cell, what happens? (one of 4 points)
2017-Q14a.right: They assemble and burst out of the cell
wrong: They divide in two by binary fission
They form endospores inside the cell
They turn the host into a new virus
2017-Q14a.why: Any four: virus attaches; injects nucleic acid; uses host structures to copy its parts; parts assemble; new viruses are released.
2017-Q14a.hint: Follow a virus from landing on a cell to new viruses leaving it. What happens at each step?

2017-Q14a.q: Why are viruses not considered living organisms? (2 points)
2017-Q14a.right: Can't reproduce on their own; not made of cells
wrong: Have no DNA or RNA; not made of cells
Reproduce by binary fission; have no nucleus
Can't reproduce alone; are single cells with no nucleus
2017-Q14a.why: Two points: viruses can't reproduce independently (only inside a host cell), and they are non-cellular.
2017-Q14a.hint: Run a virus through the features all living things share. Which ones does it fail?

2017-Q14b.q: Who is most at risk in a measles outbreak?
wrong: People who had measles as children
People fully vaccinated with MMR
People who recently took antibiotics
2017-Q14b.why: Unvaccinated people (and babies too young for the jab) have no antibodies or memory cells for measles.
2017-Q14b.hint: Who would have no antibodies or memory cells for measles at all?

2017-Q14b.q: What is a vaccine and how does it give immunity? (3 points)
2017-Q14b.right: Harmless dose of pathogen; its antigen stimulates antibodies
wrong: Ready-made antibodies; they kill the pathogen straight away
Harmless dose of pathogen; antigen stimulates antibiotics
A drug that kills pathogens; it stops antigens forming
2017-Q14b.why: Three points: a vaccine is a harmless dose of a pathogen; it brings in the antigen, which stimulates the body to produce antibodies.
2017-Q14b.hint: First, what's in the jab (is the germ harmful?), then what your lymphocytes do when they meet it.

2017-Q14b.q: Which list has three types of T lymphocyte?
wrong: Killer, helper, monocyte
Helper, B cell, killer
Suppressor, phagocyte, memory
2017-Q14b.why: T cells come as helper, killer, suppressor and memory; B cells, monocytes and phagocytes are other white cells.
2017-Q14b.hint: T cells are named for their jobs, like a team: a supporter, a fighter, a referee, a record keeper.

2017-Q14b.q: What is the role of helper T cells? (one of 3 points)
2017-Q14b.right: Stimulate B cells to make antibodies
wrong: Burst infected cells with perforin
Switch off the immune response
Make antibodies against antigens
2017-Q14b.why: Three points: a role for each T cell, e.g. helper T cells stimulate B cells and killer T cells; they don't make antibodies themselves.
2017-Q14b.hint: Let each name guide you, then think of the start, the fight and the end of an immune response.

2018-Q13a.q: Which entities contain only one type of nucleic acid?
wrong: Bacteria
Prions
Yeasts
2018-Q13a.why: A virus has either DNA or RNA, never both; bacteria and yeasts have both, and prions have none.
2018-Q13a.hint: Which tiny non-cellular agents are just genes wrapped in a coat of protein?

2018-Q15a.right: Resistant strains of bacteria build up
wrong: Your body becomes immune to the drug
Viruses become resistant to them
They stop your body making antibodies
2018-Q15a.why: Each course kills sensitive bacteria and leaves resistant ones to multiply, so the antibiotic stops working.
2018-Q15a.hint: Each course kills most bacteria, but not always all of them. What happens with the survivors?

2018-Q15b.q: Why does active immunity last a long time?
wrong: Antibodies are given ready-made
Antibiotics stay in the blood for years
Antigens stay in the body for life
2018-Q15b.why: Your own lymphocytes make antibodies and memory cells, which stay for years and respond fast to the same antigen.
2018-Q15b.hint: In active immunity your own cells respond. What do they leave behind for next time?

2018-Q15b.q: Why aren't antibiotics given to treat flu directly?
2018-Q15b.right: Flu is a virus; antibiotics don't affect viruses
wrong: Flu bacteria are all resistant already
Antibiotics would destroy flu antibodies
Antibiotics only work with a flu vaccine
2018-Q15b.why: Influenza is a virus and antibiotics only act on bacteria (and fungi); they could also kill useful bacteria.
2018-Q15b.hint: Is flu caused by a bacterium or something else? Then ask what antibiotics actually attack.

2019-Q14b.q: What is vaccination and what does it do? (3 points)
2019-Q14b.right: Harmless pathogen given; makes antibodies and memory cells
wrong: Ready-made antibodies given; lifelong passive immunity
Full-strength pathogen given; makes antibiotics
Harmless pathogen given; makes antibiotics to kill it
2019-Q14b.why: Three points: a harmless (weakened or dead) pathogen is given, and it stimulates antibodies and memory cells, giving active immunity.
2019-Q14b.hint: Cover what is injected, what your lymphocytes make in reply, and why the protection lasts.

2019-Q14b.q: Write about antibiotic resistance in bacteria. (3 points)
2019-Q14b.right: Mutant bacteria aren't killed by antibiotics; due to overuse
wrong: Patients become immune to antibiotics; due to overuse
Mutant bacteria aren't killed; due to finishing courses
Antibiotics mutate and stop working; due to vaccines
2019-Q14b.why: Three points: resistant bacteria aren't affected by antibiotics; they arise by mutation; overuse or not finishing a course lets them spread.
2019-Q14b.hint: Think what antibiotics fail to do to them, how they first arise, and which habits help them spread.

2020-Q15b.q: What are viral coats made of?
wrong: Lipid
Cellulose
Nucleic acid
2020-Q15b.why: Viral coats (capsids) are protein, which is why HPV coat particles can act as antigens in the vaccine.
2020-Q15b.hint: Think of which biomolecule makes enzymes and antibodies: viral coats are made of it too.

2020-Q15b.q: Besides protein, what is the other main part of a virus?
wrong: Lipid
Carbohydrate
Amino acids
2020-Q15b.why: A virus is protein plus nucleic acid, either DNA or RNA, which carries its genes; amino acids just build protein.
2020-Q15b.hint: Inside the coat are the virus's genes. What kind of molecule carries genes?

2020-Q15b.right: They can only reproduce in a host cell
wrong: They can reproduce in soil or water
They must feed on dead material
They need oxygen to survive
2020-Q15b.why: 'Obligate' means they must have a host: a virus can only make copies of itself inside a living cell.
2020-Q15b.hint: A virus has no machinery of its own. So where must it be to make more of itself?

2020-Q15b.q: Describe how a virus infects and replicates in a host cell. (3 points)
2020-Q15b.right: Attaches, injects nucleic acid, host cell makes new viruses
wrong: Attaches, injects nucleic acid, divides by binary fission
Enters the cell, uses its own ribosomes to make new viruses
Attaches, injects its protein coat, host makes new viruses
2020-Q15b.why: Three points: the virus attaches to the cell, injects its nucleic acid, and uses the host's structures to make and assemble new viruses.
2020-Q15b.hint: Start with the virus landing on the cell; then what it sends inside, and who does the copying.

2020-Q15b.q: What are the two types of induced immunity?
wrong: General and specific
Innate and inherited
B cell and T cell
2020-Q15b.why: Induced immunity is active (you make antibodies) or passive (you get them); general and specific are defence systems.
2020-Q15b.hint: Do you make the antibodies yourself, or are they given to you? Each way has a name.

2020-Q15b.q: Which type of immunity follows the HPV vaccine?
wrong: Passive
Innate
Inherited
2020-Q15b.why: The vaccine's coat proteins are antigens, so your own body makes antibodies and memory cells: active immunity.
2020-Q15b.hint: The vaccine has coat particles only. Does your body then make its own antibodies?

2020-Q15b.q: How does active immunity differ from passive?
wrong: Active immunity works faster at first
Active immunity uses donated antibodies
Active immunity makes no memory cells
2020-Q15b.why: Active immunity makes memory cells, so it lasts years; passive works at once but fades within weeks or months.
2020-Q15b.hint: Think about memory cells: which type makes them, and what does that mean over time?

2021-Q16c.q: Name two places in the body with mucous membrane linings. (2 points)
wrong: Respiratory tract and outer skin
Inside arteries and bone marrow
Digestive tract and inside bones
2021-Q16c.why: Two points: any two of the respiratory, digestive and reproductive tracts (tubes open to the outside), not the skin or blood vessels.
2021-Q16c.hint: Think of tubes that open to the outside world: where air goes in, and where food goes.

wrong: Pancreas
Kidneys
Thyroid gland
2021-Q16c.why: All lymphocytes are made in the bone marrow; T cells then move to the thymus to mature.
2021-Q16c.hint: All blood cells, red and white, start out in the same soft tissue. Where is it?

2021-Q16c.q: Which type of lymphocyte produces antibodies?
wrong: Helper T cells
Killer T cells
Memory T cells
2021-Q16c.why: B lymphocytes make antibodies; helper T cells only stimulate them, and killer T cells attack infected cells.
2021-Q16c.hint: Memory hook: its letter matches where it matures, the soft tissue deep inside your bones.

2021-Q16c.q: Which white blood cell, other than a lymphocyte, fights infection?
wrong: Helper T cell
B lymphocyte
Platelet
2021-Q16c.why: Macrophages (from monocytes) are phagocytes that engulf microbes; B and T cells are lymphocytes.
2021-Q16c.hint: Think of the large white cells that swallow microbes whole by phagocytosis.

2021-Q16c.q: From the graph, how does the response at B compare with A?
2021-Q16c.right: B is faster and makes more antibodies
wrong: B is slower and makes fewer antibodies
B is faster but makes fewer antibodies
B is slower but makes more antibodies
2021-Q16c.why: After the vaccine (A) antibodies rose slowly and only a little; after infection (B) they rose fast and much higher.
2021-Q16c.hint: Compare the two curves: how quickly does each one rise, and how high does each one peak?

2021-Q16c.q: Why was the antibody response at B faster and bigger?
2021-Q16c.right: Memory cells from the vaccine were present
wrong: The person had no memory cells by B
The vaccine gave passive immunity
Antibiotics boosted antibodies at B
2021-Q16c.why: The vaccine left memory cells, so the second meeting with the antigen got a fast, strong response.
2021-Q16c.hint: What did the vaccine at A leave behind that was ready and waiting by B?

2021-Q16c.q: Which part of the virus do antibodies recognise?
wrong: The RNA inside the coat
The virus's cell wall
The virus's ribosomes
2021-Q16c.why: Antibodies bind antigens on the surface, which are coat proteins (like the spike); the RNA is hidden inside.
2021-Q16c.hint: Antibodies can only reach what is on the outside. What is the outside of a virus made of?

2021-Q16c.right: Antibiotics have no effect on viruses
wrong: COVID-19 bacteria are all resistant
Antibiotics stop the vaccine working
The virus breaks down antibiotics
2021-Q16c.why: COVID-19 is caused by a virus, and antibiotics act only on bacteria (and fungi), not viruses.
2021-Q16c.hint: What kind of microbe causes COVID-19, and which kinds of microbe do antibiotics act on?

2022-Q5d.q: True or false: macrophages are white blood cells that secrete perforin.
wrong: True
2022-Q5d.why: Macrophages engulf microbes by phagocytosis; perforin is released by killer T cells.
2022-Q5d.hint: Think about how macrophages kill: do they eat microbes, or punch holes in infected cells?

2022-Q7.q: What is molecule A on the diagram?
wrong: Protein
Lipid
Cellulose
2022-Q7.why: A is the genetic material inside the virus: a nucleic acid, which in SARS-CoV-2 is RNA.
2022-Q7.hint: A sits in the core and carries the virus's genes. What type of molecule does that job?

2022-Q7.q: Where should the arrow from X point to show an antigen?
2022-Q7.right: A protein on the outer surface
wrong: The RNA in the core of the virus
The inner side of the protein coat
The empty space inside the virus
2022-Q7.why: Antigens are the surface proteins (spikes) that antibodies recognise, so they're on the outside of the virus.
2022-Q7.hint: Antibodies grab antigens, so they must be reachable. Look at what sticks out of the virus.

2022-Q7.q: What makes a virus an obligate parasite?
2022-Q7.right: It needs a host cell to reproduce
wrong: It can reproduce by itself in water
It feeds on dead organic matter
It makes its own food from light
2022-Q7.why: Viruses have no machinery of their own, so they cannot replicate outside a living host cell.
2022-Q7.hint: Think of what a virus can't do on its own, and what it needs to borrow to do it.

2022-Q7.q: Explain in detail the term vaccination. (2 points)
2022-Q7.right: Giving a harmless dose of pathogen to stimulate antibodies
wrong: Giving ready-made antibodies to fight a pathogen
Taking antibiotics to kill a pathogen before infection
Giving a harmless pathogen to stimulate antibiotics
2022-Q7.why: Two points: a harmless (dead, weakened or part) dose of the pathogen is given, and it stimulates the body to produce antibodies.
2022-Q7.hint: Think of what's in the jab and whether it can make you ill, then what your body makes in reply.

2022-Q7.q: Which of these is a harmful virus?
wrong: MRSA
Salmonella
E. coli
2022-Q7.why: HIV is a virus that attacks the immune system; MRSA, Salmonella and harmful E. coli are all bacteria.
2022-Q7.hint: Think of a virus behind an illness you've been vaccinated for, or one that attacks immune cells.

2022-Q7.q: Which is a beneficial use of a virus?
wrong: Making penicillin to treat infections
Brewing beer by fermentation
Breaking down sewage
2022-Q7.why: Phages are viruses that kill bacteria; penicillin, brewing and sewage treatment use fungi or bacteria instead.
2022-Q7.hint: Some viruses only infect bacteria, and all viruses can carry genes. How might that help us?

2022-Q11b.q: Give any two examples of harmful bacteria. (2 points)
wrong: Salmonella and influenza
MRSA and Rhizobium
Penicillium and MRSA
2022-Q11b.why: Two points: any two harmful bacteria, e.g. Salmonella and MRSA; flu is a virus, Penicillium a fungus, and Rhizobium is helpful.
2022-Q11b.hint: Think of bugs behind food poisoning, or a hospital 'superbug' that shrugs off antibiotics.

2022-Q11b.right: A chemical that kills or slows bacteria
wrong: A protein your body makes against antigens
A weakened bacterium that gives immunity
A chemical that kills viruses in cells
2022-Q11b.why: Antibiotics kill or stop the growth of bacteria; they don't work on viruses, and antibodies are your own proteins.
2022-Q11b.hint: Think of penicillin from a doctor: what does it do to the bacteria causing an infection?

2022-Q11b.q: What is one reason antibiotic resistance has arisen?
wrong: Too many people being vaccinated
Bacteria learning from antibodies
Antibiotics being used too rarely
2022-Q11b.why: Overuse lets resistant mutants survive while the others die, so they multiply and take over.
2022-Q11b.hint: Think about human habits with antibiotics: how often, and how carefully, are they taken?

2022-Q17b.q: State two biological benefits of breastfeeding. (2 points)
wrong: Balanced nutrients, and lifelong active immunity
Antibiotics for the baby, and ovulation returns sooner
Antibodies, and the mother ovulates sooner
2022-Q17b.why: Two points: breast milk gives a balanced supply of nutrients and passes on antibodies (passive immunity); it's also at the right temperature.
2022-Q17b.hint: Think of the milk as both a meal and a medicine: what does each side give the baby?

2023-Q5e.q: Which of these is a harmful bacterium?
wrong: Rhizobium
Penicillium
Influenza
2023-Q5e.why: Staphylococcus causes skin and wound infections (e.g. MRSA); Rhizobium is helpful, and the others aren't bacteria.
2023-Q5e.hint: Think of a bacterium that causes food poisoning, wound infections or a sore throat.

2023-Q6e.q: Why don't doctors give antibiotics for a viral infection?
2023-Q6e.right: Antibiotics only kill bacteria and fungi
wrong: Antibiotics make viruses multiply faster
Viruses need a higher dose of antibiotic
Antibiotics destroy the body's antibodies
2023-Q6e.why: Antibiotics target bacteria (and fungi); viruses have none of the parts antibiotics attack, so they're unaffected.
2023-Q6e.hint: Antibiotics attack parts like bacterial cell walls and ribosomes. Does a virus have those?

2023-Q11b.q: What relationship is there between ash trees and the pathogen?
wrong: Mutualism
Competition
Predation
2023-Q11b.why: The fungus lives on the ash tree and harms it, which is parasitism; in mutualism both partners benefit.

2023-Q11b.q: How could ecologists help ash trees survive in Ireland?
2023-Q11b.right: Keep a gene bank of resistant ash trees
wrong: Vaccinate the ash trees against it
Plant more ash from continental Europe
Remove the moths that feed on ash
2023-Q11b.why: Tolerant trees can be stored in a gene bank and bred for planting; imported plants brought the disease in.
2023-Q11b.hint: Some ash trees cope with the disease. How could ecologists save and spread those trees?

2023-Q16c.q: On the diagram, what is structure X?
wrong: Nucleic acid
Cell wall
Cell membrane
2023-Q16c.why: X is the outer protein coat (capsid); the nucleic acid, Y, is the genetic material inside it.
2023-Q16c.hint: X is the outer shell and Y the genetic core. What is each one made of?

2023-Q16c.q: Why is it hard to describe viruses as living?
2023-Q16c.right: They have no metabolism of their own
wrong: They are made of many cells
They contain no protein at all
They can grow and respire alone
2023-Q16c.why: Viruses are non-cellular with no metabolism; they only show signs of life inside a host cell.
2023-Q16c.hint: Think of the basic unit every living thing is built from. Is a virus built from it?

wrong: Hepatitis B virus and Salmonella
HIV and Penicillium
Tetanus and TB bacteria
2023-Q16c.why: Two points: any two harmful viruses, e.g. HIV, hepatitis, flu or cold viruses; Salmonella, tetanus and TB are bacteria, Penicillium a fungus.
2023-Q16c.hint: Think of virus illnesses you've had or heard of: winter ones, pandemics, ones that hit the liver.

2023-Q16c.q: How can viruses be useful to humans?
wrong: To make antibiotics
To ferment sugar into alcohol
To fix nitrogen in soil
2023-Q16c.why: Viruses are used to make vaccines and as gene vectors; antibiotics, alcohol and nitrogen fixing use fungi or bacteria.
2023-Q16c.hint: Think of how a virus delivers genes into cells, and how scientists might borrow that skill.

2023-Q16c.q: Which of these is a SPECIFIC defence against viruses? (one of 4 points)
2023-Q16c.right: Killer T cells destroy infected cells
wrong: Skin acts as a barrier to entry
Mucus traps the virus particles
Phagocytes engulf infected cells
2023-Q16c.why: Four points: two general (e.g. skin is a barrier, mucus traps them) and two specific (e.g. antibodies, killer T cells kill infected cells).
2023-Q16c.hint: General defences block or eat any germ. Specific ones use lymphocytes and what they make.

wrong: Able to form endospores
Able to make antibiotics
Able to fix nitrogen
2024-Q14b.why: A pathogenic bacterium causes disease; forming endospores or making antibiotics doesn't make it a pathogen.
2024-Q14b.hint: Think of the opposite of a harmless gut bacterium. What do pathogenic ones do to their host?

2024-Q14b.q: What can misusing antibiotics lead to?
wrong: Antibiotic-resistant viruses
Lifelong immunity to bacteria
A lack of antibodies in blood
2024-Q14b.why: Misuse kills sensitive bacteria and leaves resistant ones to multiply, so infections get harder to treat.
2024-Q14b.hint: If antibiotics are overused, which bacteria are left alive to multiply?

2024-Q14c.q: Why is it hard to describe viruses as living organisms?
2024-Q14c.right: They are not made of cells
wrong: They are made of a single cell
They have DNA but no protein
They feed on dead organic matter
2024-Q14c.why: Viruses aren't cells and have no metabolism, so they break the rule that living things are made of cells.
2024-Q14c.hint: Living things are built from tiny units with a membrane and cytoplasm. Does a virus have them?

2024-Q14c.q: Which two biochemicals make up all viruses?
wrong: Lipid and carbohydrate
Cellulose and chitin
Phospholipid and starch
2024-Q14c.why: Every virus is a protein coat around nucleic acid (DNA or RNA); some also have a fatty envelope, but not all.
2024-Q14c.hint: Every virus has an outer shell and a genetic core. Which biomolecule makes up each?

2024-Q14c.q: Which is the right order for viral replication?
wrong: Inject, attach, assemble, copy, release
Attach, copy, inject, release, assemble
Attach, inject, release, copy, assemble
2024-Q14c.why: A virus attaches, injects its nucleic acid, uses the host to copy its parts, assembles new viruses and releases them.
2024-Q14c.hint: Think of the virus as a hijacker: how does it get in, use the cell, and then leave?

2024-Q14c.q: Which of these is a harmful virus?
wrong: Streptococcus
Listeria
Penicillium
2024-Q14c.why: Coronaviruses cause colds and COVID-19; Streptococcus and Listeria are bacteria and Penicillium is a fungus.
2024-Q14c.hint: Think of a virus that has made the news, or one that gives you sniffles every winter.

2024-Q14c.q: Which is a way viruses can be beneficial?
2024-Q14c.right: As vectors to carry genes into cells
wrong: As a source of penicillin
As decomposers in the soil
By fixing nitrogen for plants
2024-Q14c.why: Viruses naturally carry genes into cells, so they're used as vectors in genetic engineering and gene therapy.
2024-Q14c.hint: Some viruses kill bacteria, and all are good at getting into cells. How might scientists use that?

2024-Q16d.q: Name two methods used by the general defence system. (2 points)
wrong: Skin as a barrier; antibodies from B cells
Phagocytosis; killer T cells
Memory cells; antibody production
2024-Q16d.why: Two points: any two general defences, e.g. skin barrier, phagocytosis, stomach acid, fever or clotting; antibodies and T cells are specific.
2024-Q16d.hint: Think of what stops germs getting in at all, and what happens to germs that do get in.

2024-Q16d.q: Which organ is specific to the immune system?
wrong: Liver
Pancreas
Thyroid
2024-Q16d.why: The spleen filters blood and holds lymphocytes; the liver, pancreas and thyroid have other jobs.
2024-Q16d.hint: Think of the organ beside the stomach, on the left, that filters old red cells from the blood.

2024-Q16d.q: Distinguish between an antigen and an antibody. (2 points)
2024-Q16d.right: Antigen triggers antibodies, proteins made in response to it
wrong: Antibody triggers antigens, proteins made in response to it
Antigen is a fungal drug; antibody is a protein on microbes
Antigen is a weakened microbe; antibody is an antibiotic
2024-Q16d.why: Two points: an antigen is a molecule (e.g. on a microbe) that stimulates antibody production; an antibody is a protein made in response.

2024-Q16d.q: Besides T cells, what is the other type of lymphocyte?
wrong: Monocytes
Macrophages
Platelets
2024-Q16d.why: Lymphocytes are B cells and T cells; monocytes and macrophages are phagocytes, and platelets help clotting.
2024-Q16d.hint: T cells mature in the thymus. The other kind matures in the bone marrow: which letter is it?

2024-Q16d.q: What is the role of memory T cells? (one of 4 points)
2024-Q16d.right: Remember an antigen for a faster response
wrong: Burst infected cells using perforin
Switch off the immune response
Make antibodies to the antigen
2024-Q16d.why: Four points: name two T cells and a job for each, e.g. killer T cells burst infected cells; memory T cells remember the antigen.
2024-Q16d.hint: Each of the four is named after its job: think of rallying, attacking, calling a halt and recall.

2025-Q16d.q: Name two organs of the lymphatic system. (2 points)
wrong: Lymph nodes and thyroid
Spleen and pancreas
Kidneys and adrenals
2025-Q16d.why: Two points: any two of lymph nodes, spleen, thymus, tonsils, adenoids and lymph vessels; the thyroid, pancreas and kidneys aren't lymphatic.
2025-Q16d.hint: Think of the lumps that swell in your neck when you're sick, and an organ that filters blood.

2025-Q16d.q: Other than maturing lymphocytes, give two functions of the lymphatic system. (2 points)
2025-Q16d.right: Returns tissue fluid to the blood; transports fats
wrong: Returns fluid to the blood; carries oxygen to cells
Transports fats; pumps blood around the body
Makes bile to digest fats; makes insulin
2025-Q16d.why: Two points: it returns tissue fluid to the blood and transports fats from the gut; it also helps fight infection.
2025-Q16d.hint: Think of fluid that leaks out of capillaries, and what lacteals in the villi absorb.

2025-Q16d.q: Where exactly in the body are lymphocytes made?
wrong: Pancreas
Kidneys
Thyroid gland
2025-Q16d.why: Lymphocytes are made in the bone marrow; the thymus is only where T cells go to mature.
2025-Q16d.hint: It's the same soft tissue that makes your red blood cells. Where is that found?

2025-Q16d.q: Name two lymphocytes and describe the role of each. (4 points)
2025-Q16d.right: B cells make antibodies; killer T cells destroy infected cells
wrong: B cells engulf microbes; killer T cells make antibodies
Helper T cells make antibodies; B cells burst infected cells
Monocytes engulf microbes; platelets destroy infected cells
2025-Q16d.why: Four points: two lymphocytes named, each with its role: B cells make antibodies; killer T cells destroy infected cells (helper T cells switch them on).
2025-Q16d.hint: Think of the two lettered kinds: which releases Y-shaped proteins, and which attacks directly?

2025-Q16d.right: Giving a harmless antigen to trigger immunity
wrong: Giving antibodies for instant immunity
Giving antibiotics to prevent infection
Giving a full dose of a live pathogen
2025-Q16d.why: Vaccination brings in a weakened or harmless pathogen or antigen so your body builds active immunity.
2025-Q16d.hint: Think of what goes into the body in the jab, whether it can make you sick, and what it sets off.

2026-Q16b.q: Which pair names X and Y on diagram 1?
wrong: X nucleic acid, Y protein
X lipid, Y protein
X lipid, Y carbohydrate
2026-Q16b.why: X is the protein coat and Y is the genetic material inside it, DNA or RNA; every virus has both.
2026-Q16b.hint: X wraps around the outside and Y carries the genes. Which biomolecule makes up each?

2026-Q16b.q: Apart from round, what other shape can a virus be?
wrong: Comma-shaped
Chain of spheres
Grape-like cluster
2026-Q16b.why: Viruses can be round, rod-shaped or complex (like phages); comma, chain and cluster shapes describe bacteria.
2026-Q16b.hint: Picture tobacco mosaic virus under an electron microscope: long, thin and straight.

2026-Q16b.q: In diagram 2, how does the virus use the host cell? (one of 4 points)
2026-Q16b.right: Uses its organelles to copy viral parts
wrong: Splits in two inside it by binary fission
Uses its own ribosomes inside the cell
Forms spores inside it that later hatch
2026-Q16b.why: Any four: its DNA or RNA enters; it uses host organelles; makes viral nucleic acid and protein; parts assemble; new viruses are released.
2026-Q16b.hint: The virus brings only its genes. Whose ribosomes and materials build the new parts, and then what?

2026-Q16b.q: Why is a red blood cell a poor host for viruses?
2026-Q16b.right: It has no nucleus or organelles
wrong: It has a thick cell wall
It is full of antibodies
Its nucleus destroys viral DNA
2026-Q16b.why: A mature red cell has no nucleus or organelles, so a virus has no machinery to hijack for copying itself.
2026-Q16b.hint: A virus needs the cell's machinery to copy itself. What does a mature red cell lack?

2026-Q16b.q: State two examples of harmful viruses. (2 points)
wrong: HIV and Salmonella
Flu virus and Penicillium
Cholera and tetanus
2026-Q16b.why: Two points: any two harmful viruses, e.g. HIV and flu; Salmonella, cholera and tetanus are bacteria, and Penicillium is a fungus.
2026-Q16b.hint: Think of a virus that attacks immune cells, or ones behind the illnesses you're vaccinated against.

2026-Q16b.q: Which is a beneficial use of viruses?
2026-Q16b.right: Gene therapy: carrying genes into cells
wrong: Producing penicillin for medicine
Turning milk into cheese
Decomposing dead leaves
2026-Q16b.why: Viruses can deliver genes into cells for gene therapy; penicillin, cheese and decay rely on fungi or bacteria.
2026-Q16b.hint: Viruses are good at getting into cells. What could doctors or scientists send in with them?

S1-Q3b.q: What is the main role of monocytes in innate immunity? (2 points)
wrong: Make antibodies against one antigen
Burst infected cells using perforin
Remember antigens for next time
S1-Q3b.why: Two points: monocytes (macrophages) engulf any pathogen or dust by phagocytosis and digest it with lysosome enzymes: a non-specific defence.
S1-Q3b.hint: Think of what this cell does when it meets dust or a bacterium in the air sac.

S1-Q3b.right: Inflammation brings more phagocytes to a site
wrong: B cells making antibodies to an antigen
Memory cells forming after a vaccine
Killer T cells attacking a virus
S1-Q3b.why: In inflammation, histamine widens blood vessels so more phagocytes arrive; antibodies and T cells are specific.
S1-Q3b.hint: Think of any defence that works the same on every germ: barriers, chemicals, or the body's heat.

S2-Q1b.q: Why test the vaccine on people from all over the world?
S2-Q1b.right: Genes and virus strains vary, so results apply worldwide
wrong: So no placebo group was needed, saving time and money
To make the trial double-blind and use fewer people
Everyone reacts the same, so it just speeds up the trial
S2-Q1b.why: People's genes differ and virus strains vary from place to place, so a worldwide sample gives results that apply to everyone.
S2-Q1b.hint: Think about how people, and the virus itself, might differ from one country to another.

S2-Q1b.right: Control group got a dummy jab, to compare with vaccine group
wrong: Everyone got the vaccine, but at different doses to compare
Control group got antibodies; any difference is due to them
Control group got a weaker vaccine to find the best dose
S2-Q1b.why: Two points: a control group got an identical injection with no vaccine, to compare with the vaccine group; any difference is due to the vaccine.
S2-Q1b.hint: What did the 21 728 people who didn't get the vaccine receive, and why compare them?

S2-Q1b.q: Comment on the sample of 43 448 people in terms of reliability. (2 points)
S2-Q1b.right: Large sample: more reliable, as it cuts the effect of chance
wrong: Large sample: less reliable, as more mistakes creep in
Sample size has no effect; only the number of doses does
Large sample: more reliable, as everyone reacts the same
S2-Q1b.why: Two points: a large sample makes the data more reliable, because it cuts out the effect of chance and odd individual results.
S2-Q1b.hint: Is 43 448 big or small? Think what a few odd results would do to a tiny sample.

S2-Q1b.q: Can we conclude the vaccine works for under-16s?
S2-Q1b.right: No: only people 16 or over were tested
wrong: Yes: 95% protection applies to everyone
Yes: children have stronger immune systems
Yes: the sample size was very large
S2-Q1b.why: The trial only included people aged 16 or over, so you can't extend the result to children without testing them.
S2-Q1b.hint: Look at the ages of the people who took part in the trial. Who was left out?

S2-Q1e.q: Explain why prions can be classed as pathogens. (2 points)
S2-Q1e.right: They cause disease (BSE, CJD) and are infectious
wrong: They are living cells that reproduce by dividing in two
They contain DNA that they inject into host cells
They are a type of virus with a protein coat
S2-Q1e.why: Two points: prions cause disease (like BSE and CJD), and they are infectious, making normal proteins misfold into more prions.
S2-Q1e.hint: Recall what 'pathogen' means, then check the passage for what prions do and how they spread.

S2-Q1e.q: How could BSE prions pass from cattle to humans?
wrong: Mosquito bites after biting cattle
Breathing in air near infected cattle
Touching the skin of infected cattle
S2-Q1e.why: vCJD came from eating infected beef products, especially brain or spinal cord tissue where prions build up.
S2-Q1e.hint: How do most people come into contact with cattle? Think about what ends up on the dinner plate.

S2-Q1e.q: Explain the importance of folding in proteins. (2 points)
S2-Q1e.right: Gives its specific 3D shape, which decides its function
wrong: Stores its genetic code, and the code decides its function
Joins amino acids by peptide bonds to make the chain
Stops it ever denaturing, so it works at any temperature
S2-Q1e.why: Two points: folding gives a protein its specific 3D shape (like an active site), and that shape decides its function; misfolded ones fail.
S2-Q1e.hint: Think of an enzyme's active site: what does folding give a protein, and why does that matter?

wrong: Bacterium
Fungus
Protist
S2-Q1e.why: Viruses, like prions, aren't made of cells; bacteria, fungi and protists are all cellular.
S2-Q1e.hint: Which disease agent is just genes in a protein coat, with no cell at all?
